superficial: A sheet from the Transit Council, bound in blue leather and sealed with seven diamonds in a row.
“The incidents reported at distant Gates are isolated and within what was expected. There is no risk to transit. Business will proceed as normal.”
In the margin, in small cramped writing: “Expected by whom?”
A whole wall of index cards, one column for each subject: Gates, Crossings, Clocks, Tides…
Three columns are empty. They are not missing ink; they are missing everything. Where the cards would go, the same label: “See Sealed Room.”
Someone has written underneath, in pencil: “Debt — see Sealed Room.” And again, pressing harder: “Debt — see Sealed Room.”
Dozens of clocks on the walls, in every size. Each carries a label with the place where it was calibrated: Workshop, Threshold, Scar…
They were all set to the same hour at once. They no longer agree, and without any sums you can see how far each has drifted from the one in Threshold: just put them side by side.
profunda: There is one clock with no world on its label, on the far wall. Its hand has barely moved: for every five turns of the Threshold clock, it makes one.
Now I know what I am looking at: the clock of a place where time hardly runs.

superficial: Four sheets on the long table, with no envelopes and in no order. Each is dated with the day of a different clock, and the replies seem to arrive before the questions.
They would have to be put in a row by when each was written, not by the date it carries.
profunda: Put in their places, the sheets tell something else: the researcher’s report was filed three times, and each time something was erased before it was put away.
The dates do not lie: each was written on a clock that ran at its own pace. The same happens to anything that crosses from one mouth to another: it arrives from an age that is not its own.

superficial: The archivist’s desk: a lamp with no oil, a dry cup and an open notebook with notes in the margins, almost all of them questions.
“At four, the light of the Ember comes in through the slot and wanders over the tablet at the back. You have to read it at once: it lasts an hour and a half.”
profunda: “There are forty days I do not remember filing. The cards are in my handwriting. So are the dates.”
“Someone lives in another time and sends me things, and I file them without knowing when they arrived.”

superficial: A stone tablet with a map of the sky: dots for the stars and, in the middle, a dark circle.
Each star is drawn twice, once with a firm line and once with a broken one, and a curved arrow joins them.
profunda: With what I know about the Slow Site, the tablet explains itself: the broken dots are where each star is and the firm ones, where it is seen. Near the dark circle, the two positions drift far apart.
The circle is something enormously heavy that bends light. Whatever is seen near it is not where it seems.

superficial: In the darkest part of the canyon, records marked “closed.” Minutes of the Transit Council, one after another.
“A vote is put on whether to report the risk to the inhabited Gates. Result: it is not reported.”
At the bottom, the signature: seven diamonds in a row.
profunda: Among the minutes there is an order of another kind, with nobody’s name on it: “Let an apparatus be built that holds the last quarter hour of the Mouth.”
Nobody writes down what for. The next entry is a bill of materials.

superficial: A small bronze sphere with a cogwheel carved around it.
It weighs little and tinkles: something turns inside.
An ember-colored sphere with a piece missing: a clean, round cut, like those in the ground of a world.
A water-colored sphere with a point on top: a drop about to fall.
A pale sand sphere surrounded by a thin ring: the ring of a Gate.
A pearl half-sphere on a flat base: a dome, like those that watch the sky.
A round table with six golden rails, one inside another, and a crank. At the center, a small sun.
Each rail has a socket for a sphere. Five are gold. The fifth is black, and empty.
A glass prism lying on the floor, with a notch in its base. It seems to have fallen from its stand.
A steel post with a golden ring on top, beside the tablet of the light slot. Something was meant to go here.

archivo.cisterna.titulo: The cistern of the Canyon Floor
superficial: A waist-high stone basin, with a pumice barge floating on the water. On the barge, record drawers locked shut.
On the wall of the basin there are three gold marks, one above another. Above the last, the mouth of an overflow.
A pile of small gray stone blocks, each of a single part.
A pile of medium gray stone blocks, each of two parts, marked with two stripes.
A pile of large gray stone blocks, each of three parts, marked with three stripes.
Some planks of pale, dry wood. You can tell by the water stains they left: they float.
Five copper pendulums hang from one beam. Each rod has five notches for its length, and the weight slides along it.
A copper beam from wall to wall with five pendulums hanging from it. While they swing together, the beam trembles and the latch of the hatch will not give.
Changing the weight of one does not part them. Changing the length does.
Three standing sheets of glass, each with a version of the same report. In each version there is a gap where something was erased.
Laid one after another, the gaps fill in: “The debt is one of time.” “The Limit drops with every new Gate.” “Estimated date: within this year.”
A sheet nailed to the wall, signed with two signs: a diamond with a dot and a downward triangle. The researcher and the skeptic.
“Do not evacuate through the Gates. Every departure adds to the count. Stay and wait for the Counterweight.”
Above it, a red seal of seven diamonds in a row: “File it away.”
A small beam with dozens of tiny pendulums, one for each Gate. Almost all hang together.
At one end one hangs apart, with a sign that is not of the Absent: two rings with a line down the middle. It is the sign of home.
